source: Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF), General Directorate of Agriculture / ASPIRE program (Agriculture Services Programme for Innovation, Resilience and Extension) - Technical Document: "Sweet Corn Cultivation Techniques Resilient to Climate Change" (បច្ចេកទេសដាំដាំណាំពោតផ្អែមធន់នឹងការប្រែប្រួលអាកាសធាតុ), 2018
text:
Corn (ពោត) has several special characteristics and can be processed into many kinds of products depending on demand. In Cambodia, farmers grow corn to feed livestock and as a supplementary food, as well as for direct human consumption — boiled, grilled/roasted, or eaten raw as a snack — and as young/baby corn. Beyond these uses, corn is also processed into preserved food for long-term storage and is exported abroad.

When selecting corn seed for planting, farmers should choose: seed suited to the local soil type and climate conditions of the area; seed with good drought tolerance; good-quality seed with a purity rate above 95%; seed with a germination rate above 85%; fresh seed that has not been stored too long (not multiple months or years old); seed resistant to disease and insect pests and that is not broken/cracked; and clean, pure seed that gives high yield and commands a good market price (such as hybrid seed sold by seed companies).

This document is a climate-change-resilient technical guideline for sweet corn (ពោតផ្អែម) cultivation produced by MAFF's General Directorate of Agriculture together with the ASPIRE program, intended as reference material for provincial, municipal, city and district-level agriculture officials, NGOs, local implementing agencies, and other stakeholders involved in transferring farming techniques and climate-risk-reduction methods to farmers, aiming to help farmers and producers achieve higher-quality yields and increased income. The document notes that climate change negatively affects agricultural production, especially rain-fed farming, and that shifting planting seasons due to climate change strongly affects corn production — increases in pest and disease outbreaks, changes in rainfall patterns, irregular rainfall, drought, and flooding all reduce corn yield and farmer income. Key practices recommended to reduce climate-related risk in corn production include: variety selection, land preparation and bed-forming, planting, crop care, pest and disease management, and crop rotation.
